e-6174.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function
e-6174.problem: A particle moves in a straight line. After $t$ seconds the particle is $\, f(t)=2t^3 - 5t + 9\,$ feet away from its initial position. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the particle's position as a function of $t?$
e-6174.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the particle's position is equal to $f'(t).$ 

We take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-5t+9) \\  & =6{t}^{2}-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, after $t$ seconds, the instantaneous rate of change of the particle's position is $6t^2 - 5$ feet per second.

e-276.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function at a Point
e-276.problem: Lizzie buys $b$ pounds of bananas at a price $p,$ in dollars, that can be modeled by the function $p(b)=5e^{-0.2b}.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of the price when $b=5$ pounds?
e-276.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the price when $b=5$ pounds is equal to $p'(5).$

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{′}(b) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}b}(5{e}^{-0.2b}) \\  & =5{e}^{-0.2b}\cdot (-0.2) \\  & =-{e}^{-0.2b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $b=5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{′}(5) & =-{e}^{-0.2(5)} \\  & =-{e}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the price when $b=5$ pounds is $-\dfrac{1}{e}$ dollars per pound.

e-275.knowledge_point: Further Determining Rates of Change in Geometrical Settings
e-275.problem:
A spherical balloon is being inflated so that its volume is increasing. Find the instantaneous rate at which the volume of the balloon is changing with respect to the radius at the moment when the diameter of the balloon is equal to $12\, \text{cm}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13948186/assets/e03fb046f74771676d7b1e83a1cf09176adcffaf8112e9de263404b8be74b026.png)
e-275.worked_solution:
Since we are given that the diameter of the balloon is $12\, \text{cm},$ its radius is $r =6\, \text{cm}.$ Now, we know that the volume of a sphere with radius $r$  is given by 

$$
V= V(r) = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3.
$$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $V(r)$  with respect to $r$ is 

$$
\eqalign{

V'(r) &= \dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d r}\left(  \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3\right)\[5pt]
 &  =  \dfrac{4}{3}\pi (3r^2)\[5pt]
 &= 4\pi r^2, 
}
$$

and evaluating at $r=6$ gives

$$
V'(6)=  4\pi (6)^2= 144\pi.
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the volume of the balloon is changing when its diameter is $12\, \text{cm}\,$ is $\, 144\pi \, \text{cm}^3/\text{cm}.$

**Note:** We read $\text{cm}^3/\text{cm}$ as "centimeters cubed per centimeter".

content.problem: The function $P(t)=710\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{e}^{t})$ represents the volume of milk, in liters, produced on a farm $t$ days after the owner bought new cows. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the volume of produced milk as a function of $t?$
content.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the volume of produced milk with respect to time is ${P}^{′}(t).$

Now, the rate of change of $P(t)$ with respect to $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(710\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{e}^{t})) \\  & =710\,\frac{{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{710}{1+{e}^{-t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change of the volume of produced milk is  $\frac{710}{1+{e}^{-t}}$ liters per day.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: The function $L(s)={s}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡s$ models the surface area of a flower's petal, in squared millimeters, as the flower's stem grows to a length of $s$ centimeters, where $s>1.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of the surface area as a function of $s?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}({s}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡s) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}({s}^{2})\operatorname{ln}⁡s+{s}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{ln}⁡s) \\  & =(2s)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡s+{s}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{s}) \\  & =2s\operatorname{ln}⁡s+s \\  & =s(2\operatorname{ln}⁡s+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the surface area is $s(2\operatorname{ln}⁡s+1)$ squared millimeters per centimeter.

The function L(s)=s2ln⁡s models the surface area of a flower's petal, in squared millimeters, as the flower's stem grows to a length of s centimeters, where s>1. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the surface area as a function of s?

a
s(2ln⁡s+1) squared millimeters per centimeter
b
2ln⁡s+1 squared millimeters per centimeter
c
1−2ln⁡s squared millimeters per centimeter
d
s2(2ln⁡s−1) squared millimeters per centimeter
e
s(ln⁡s+2) squared millimeters per centimeter
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take the derivative and get L′(s)=dds(s2ln⁡s)=dds(s2)ln⁡s+s2dds(ln⁡s)=(2s)⋅ln⁡s+s2⋅(1s)=2sln⁡s+s=s(2ln⁡s+1)

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the surface area is s(2ln⁡s+1) squared millimeters per centimeter.

content.problem: The function $L(s)={s}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡s$ models the surface area of a flower's petal, in squared millimeters, as the flower's stem grows to a length of $s$ centimeters, where $s>1.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of the surface area as a function of $s?$
content.worked_solution:
First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}({s}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡s) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}({s}^{2})\operatorname{ln}⁡s+{s}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{ln}⁡s) \\  & =(2s)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡s+{s}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{s}) \\  & =2s\operatorname{ln}⁡s+s \\  & =s(2\operatorname{ln}⁡s+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the surface area is $s(2\operatorname{ln}⁡s+1)$ squared millimeters per centimeter.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: The weight $w,$ in pounds, of a baby gorilla $t$ years after birth can be modeled by the function $w(t)=4{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+15.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of his weight when $t=1$ year?
after.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of weight when $t=1$ year is equal to ${w}^{′}(1).$

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+15) \\  & =12{t}^{2}-2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}^{′}(1) & =12(1)^{2}-2(1) \\  & =12-2 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the weight when $t=1$ year is $10$ pounds per year.

The function P(v)=2v+50v+1 models the price at which gas is sold, in dollars, depending on the volume v sold the previous day, in gallons. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the price of gas when v=5 gallons?

13 dollars per gallon
b
34 dollars per gallon
c
43 gallons per dollar
d
−34 gallons per dollar
e
−43 dollars per gallon

decision.explanation: By the quotient rule, P'(v)=[2(v+1)−(2v+50)]/(v+1)²=−48/(v+1)². Thus P'(5)=−48/36=−4/3 dollars per gallon, matching option e.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: The function $P(v)=\frac{2v+50}{v+1}$ models the price at which gas is sold, in dollars, depending on the volume $v$ sold the previous day, in gallons. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the price of gas when $v=5$ gallons?
after.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the price when $v=5$ gallons is equal to ${P}^{′}(5).$

Now, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(v) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}v}(\frac{2v+50}{v+1}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}v}(2v+50)\cdot (v+1)-(2v+50)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}v}(v+1)}{(v+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(2)\cdot (v+1)-(2v+50)\cdot (1)}{(v+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2v+2-2v-50}{(v+1)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{48}{(v+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $v=5$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(5) & =-\frac{48}{((5)+1)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{48}{36} \\  & =-\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the price when $v=5$ gallons is $-\frac{4}{3}$ dollars per gallon.

after.worked_solution:

$$
A=A(l)={l}^{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(l) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}l}({l}^{2})=2l,\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $l=6$ gives

$$
{A}^{′}(6)=2(6)=12.
$$

 

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the area of the square is increasing when the length of the side is $l=6\,\text{cm}$ is $12\,{\text{cm}}^{2}/\text{cm}.$

after.worked_solution:
The volume of the sphere is given by 

$$
V=V(r)=\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3},
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Therefore, the rate of change of $V(r)$ with respect to $r$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot 3\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
